Nearly 99% of new food ingredients haven't received formal FDA approval. And in some cases, the FDA may not even know an ingredient is being used.

It’s called GRAS, or “generally recognized as safe.”

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
Most doctors have been taught that a ketogenic diet is a fast track to a heart attack. Higher saturated fat, possible LDL rise, end of story. 
A new study in Cardiology and Therapy just tested that assumption with real patients and real outcomes instead of theory. 

Researchers examined nearly 10,000 adults with type 2 diabetes or obesity. Half (4,877) received individualized nutrition therapy through Virta’s telemedicine program targeting 30 grams of carbs or less per day and nutritional ketosis. They were matched 1:1 against 4,877 controls on usual care. Follow-up stretched up to eight years across almost 19,000 person-years. 

The researchers did not stop at risk factors or lab numbers. They looked at claims-based hard endpoints. Major cardiac events—nonfatal heart attack, stroke, or death from any cause—were 56 percent lower in the ketogenic therapy group. New-onset cardiovascular disease was 30 percent lower. Higher blood ketone levels were independently linked to lower risk, roughly 14 percent lower hazard with each step up in ketosis category. Safety data showed no increase in arrhythmias, atrial fibrillation, or prolonged QT. 

It is a retrospective matched cohort study, not a randomized trial, so it cannot prove causation by itself. Residual confounding is always possible. At the same time, the field has spent decades warning patients away from carbohydrate reduction based largely on theoretical concerns about saturated fat and LDL. Where is the randomized trial showing that modern ketogenic therapy actually raises heart attacks or strokes? When observational data with harder endpoints and better methodology points the other direction, the standard should not suddenly shift to demanding only multi-decade RCTs.

When people reverse glucotoxicity, drop triglycerides, reduce visceral fat, lower inflammation, and come off insulin and sulfonylureas, lower cardiac event rates are not surprising. This study supplies the hard-endpoint data many have asked for. Ketosis was associated with fewer cardiac events, not more. The old assumptions are starting to look a lot less solid.
hits.draft_en:
Dr Shawn Baker on the keto heart attack fear. A new study in Cardiology and Therapy looked at nearly 10,000 adults with type 2 diabetes or obesity, half on a low-carb ketogenic program, half on usual care, followed up to eight years.

Heart attack, stroke or death was 56% lower in the keto group. New heart disease was 30% lower. No rise in heart rhythm problems.

He's upfront that it's a matched cohort, not a randomised trial, so it can't prove cause. But it's hard outcomes, not just cholesterol numbers. If you're over 50 and told low carb will wreck your heart, ask to see the evidence.

Can protein cause an elevation in blood glucose? 

The answer is, it depends 

For most healthy people consuming  a moderate amount of protein the answer is generally no

However, in certain individuals protein can definitely result in blood glucose elevations 

The primary example of this is going to be someone who is metabolically unwell , which unfortunately represents the majority of the US population 

What is the mechanism? 

Primarily it will occur when the protein amounts are higher- say 50-100gms at a meal. In this instance several things are occurring. 

Certain amino acids a gluconeogenic, such as alanine and glutamine in particular, and they can cause an elevation in glucose if the amino acids availability is high enough. This can happen in the gut, the liver and in other tissues as well. 

The issue that particularly affects those who are insulin resistant or insulin deficient (eg type1 diabetics), is that proteins will stimulate both insulin from the pancreatic Beta cells as well as glucagon from the Alpha cells..  (This is why type 1 diabetics need to bolus insulin for protein and not just carbs) 

In these folks, glucagon wins that battle because insulin is compromised and thus the glucagon causes a net release of glucose into the blood stream largely coming from the breakdown of glycogen into the liver. 

How do you fix this? 

1. Fix your metabolic health-lose excess fat, get physically fit, get good sleep, manage stress, get some sunshine

2. Don’t minimize protein as that will leave you weakened and depleted, but rather break protein into smaller boluses throughout the day (a CGM in this situation may help guide on what is the appropriate amount for your metabolic state)

You’ve probably heard it: “Low-carb diets raise cortisol. They stress your adrenals. You’ll burn out.”

It sounds logical. Carbohydrates are the body’s preferred fuel, right? Cut them and your system must panic, pump out stress hormone, and eventually crash. Except the data doesn’t cooperate with the story.

In the first week or two of dropping carbs, cortisol can tick up. That’s adaptation—your body rearranging fuel lines while it learns to run on fat and ketones. The 2022 Whittaker and Harris meta-analysis of 27 studies captured exactly this: a moderate rise in resting cortisol during the first three weeks. After that, the signal disappears. 

Once you’re past the initial shift, long-term low-carb diets show no consistent elevation in resting cortisol compared with higher-carb eating.

Look further and the picture gets clearer. Eight weeks of a very-low-calorie ketogenic diet in obese men lowered salivary cortisol. Twelve weeks of a modified Atkins diet left total cortisol unchanged and reduced the free cortisol index. 

Women who had lived in nutritional ketosis for nearly four years (the KetoSAge trial) maintained healthy cortisol levels the entire time—no chronic hypercortisolemia, no adrenal “fatigue.” Even when researchers measured cortisol metabolism more carefully (Stimson et al., 2007), a high-fat, very-low-carb diet altered how the body handled the hormone but did not raise plasma levels or disrupt the normal daily rhythm.

The persistent elevation people worry about shows up mainly after long exercise sessions, which is a normal training response, not a sign that your baseline stress axis is broken.

So the narrative that chronic carbohydrate restriction keeps you in a constant cortisol emergency is largely an extrapolation from the first few weeks of change. Once adapted, resting cortisol settles back down. The body doesn’t treat sustained low-carb eating as an ongoing crisis. It treats it as a new normal.

The adrenals, it turns out, are tougher than the warnings.

Heart: WaPo's first source pooled 17 small dark chocolate trials, 615 people total. It only measured how much an artery stretched on an ultrasound. Not one heart attack, stroke or death was counted.
